items.title: Trump commercial railing against his enemies kept airing after court blocked it
items.summary: US attorney apologized to court, said government has stopped running Trump ads.
items.content:
Trump commercials paid for by the US government continued airing on TV the day after a judge blocked the ads because they likely violate a US law against government-funded publicity or propaganda.

In the most widely aired commercial, Trump railed against his perceived enemies and said he would “liberate America from these villains once and for all.” The campaign also included a commercial praising Trump’s record as president, another in which Trump calls the US the “most exceptional nation ever to exist in human history,” and commercials related to the Iran war and the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

US District Judge Jennifer Rochon issued a temporary restraining order (TRO) blocking the ads on Sunday, October 11, which took effect at 6:45 pm that night. The order said the government must cancel the ads, “including those placements for the evening of October 11, 2026.”

The Trump administration had told the court on October 10 that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) advertising purchases were set to expire on October 11 and would not be renewed. Despite that, the ads continued airing the night of October 11 and on part of October 12. This was also a week after Trump’s October 5 statement that he would start paying for the ads “myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.”

A US attorney yesterday filed a status report saying that the government is now complying with the order and issued an apology. “As Your Honor is aware, the Court emailed the TRO to the parties yesterday at 6:46 p.m.,” US Attorney Jamie McDonald wrote in a filing . “Counsel for the Government emailed the TRO to agency counsel at 7:58 p.m. Agency counsel did not become aware of Government counsel’s email until this morning. The undersigned apologizes to the Court and the plaintiffs.”

The ads aired as part of a $20 million purchase order that US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) made on September 20 with LMD Agency, an ad firm. The DHS told the court that the ad placements through October 11 cost $19 million.

In the previous Trump administration filing opposing the motion for a temporary restraining order, one of the government’s arguments was that a court order was unnecessary because the ads would not run past October 11. It said:

DHS issued a purchase order to obtain media services from a vendor in support of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) for placing national media buys. The vendor has currently purchased media buys under the terms of the purchase order through tomorrow, October 11, 2026. DHS has directed the vendor not to make any additional media buys past October 11, and DHS has no plans to make any additional media buys under the purchase order or otherwise use appropriated funds on any similar contracts for the creation or distribution of the media that is the subject of this lawsuit. Accordingly, the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow, and Plaintiffs therefore will suffer no harm, let alone irreparable harm, absent an injunction.

The Washington Post reported yesterday that the ads kept running after the restraining order took effect. Nonprofit advocacy group Common Cause and other groups that sued the government submitted a filing later in the day notifying the court of the government’s noncompliance.

The Trump ads continued airing on programs including 60 Minutes , ABC World News Tonight , and America’s Funniest Home Videos . They ran nearly 400 times after the restraining order took effect, including 32 times on Monday, according to AdImpact data cited in the plaintiffs’ court filing.

“Plaintiffs do not presently seek contempt sanctions,” the groups said. “But given that the ads have continued to run on October 12—the day after Defendants insisted the ad-buy was no longer effective—Plaintiffs request a status conference to determine Defendants’ compliance.”

After the government filed its status report, Rochon scheduled a hearing for Wednesday “to discuss this and next steps in this action.” The lawsuit is in US District Court for the Southern District of New York.

The plaintiffs are Common Cause; Robert Hunter, a Democratic candidate for a state legislature seat in Alabama; Service Employees International Union Local 32BJ; and Empire State 32BJ SEIU PAC. Defendants include DHS, the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), and the Executive Office of the President.

Rochon found that the plaintiffs are likely to succeed in their claim that the Trump administration violated the 2026 Consolidated Appropriations Act requirement that no funding may be used “for publicity or propaganda purposes within the United States not heretofore authorized by Congress.”

As of October 8, the ad “had aired approximately 9,679 times, generating an estimated 972 million impressions at an estimated cost exceeding $9.09 million,” Rochon wrote. Another $6.3 million was estimated to have been spent on four other government-funded ads challenged in the lawsuit. That’s about $15.4 million as of October 8, and more was spent over the next few days.

The temporary restraining order is in place for only two weeks, but it can be converted into a preliminary injunction that would keep the ads off the air while litigation continues. Trump, the White House, OMB, and DHS face a similar lawsuit filed by the Democratic National Committee in the federal court in the District of Columbia. A hearing on a motion for a temporary restraining order in that case is scheduled for Thursday.

items.title: Developing Gemini 4 Argon responsibly and safely
items.content:
Learn more about our approach to safety and security for Gemini 4 Argon.

VP, AI Safety & Behavior

Head of Gemini Security, Google DeepMind

Gemini 4 Argon is a step forward in what models can do — especially when it comes to deep work in complex, real-world tasks across domains including coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity, and science. Its cyberdefense capabilities are frontier-level and designed to give defenders an advantage over attackers. To maximize its potential, we first wanted cyber defenders to put it to work via our Fairwind Program , while our own security teams used it to scan critical systems inside and outside of Google.

This window of limited access showed why these capabilities matter. For instance, Wiz used Argon to uncover a critical bug in hospital software that previous models had missed, helping protect hundreds of thousands of patient records. Meanwhile, Google’s own security teams used Argon to find and patch bugs across internal software or open-source software. This included fixing foundational vulnerabilities affecting systems globally, which are going through our responsible disclosure process.

Today, we are beginning to roll out Argon broadly , as well as expanding our Fairwind Program to additional trusted cyber defenders. To do this well, we grappled with two big questions:

Our full Safety and Security Report systematically covers our set of defenses. Below are some highlights from how we approached these two questions for Gemini 4 Argon.

The same coding and reasoning improvements that enabled Argon to find and patch vulnerabilities also drove better performance on our cybersecurity tests — solving all 12 of the end-to-end simulated cyberattack scenarios, up from five in our previous generation. In biology evaluations, unguarded versions of the model also showed a much stronger ability to help troubleshoot complex lab procedures step by step. Following our Frontier Safety Framework , since we saw elevated capabilities in the cyber and biological domains, we put our next-generation set of frontier safeguards in place across both areas.

First, when it comes to potentially dangerous requests — from writing exploit code to helping with dangerous biological materials, Argon is significantly better at not fulfilling harmful requests than our previous models. On an adversarial set meant to stress test the model, violations reduced nearly twofold — also significantly better than previous Gemini models. Second, we wrap the model in three layers of real-time protection; this is to prevent determined attackers that might try to jailbreak (i.e. trick) the model by disguising a dangerous request as a harmless story or breaking it into dozens of small questions over several weeks. Here is how these protections work:

Combining real-time protection, faster fixes for new jailbreaks and enhanced monitoring for recurring misuse has made our systems better at preventing real-world harm. For instance, external bio jailbreak red teaming could only unlock less than 1% of bio sub-tasks we test for.

Misalignment can sometimes mean an agent deciding on its own to pursue a goal different to what was intended by the user. Because Argon is much better than earlier models at understanding the environment it is running in, we test carefully for that kind of behavior. For example, we ran realistic "honeypot" tests to see if the model would increase its ability to take covert actions, such as sabotaging safety monitoring. We didn't find any instances of that behavior.

But what we do see in practice today is something much more familiar: an agent trying too hard to finish the job it was given. When a resourceful assistant is told to get a task done and runs into a locked door, it can treat that obstacle as just another puzzle to solve.

This is why we trained Gemini 4 Argon to respect system boundaries, report negative findings honestly, and pause to ask for human confirmation. On coding benchmarks where models have no incentive to hold back, attempts to take a shortcut or cheat on the task dropped to just 2% on Gemini 4 Argon, our best performance for recent Gemini models.

And while this is a major step forward, when a model runs millions of complex tasks, even a rare misstep will eventually show up. As a second line of defense, we built an automated misalignment monitor that reads both the agent’s actions and its internal "scratchpad" (its step-by-step chain of thought) in real time, blocking severe boundary violations before they happen and flagging serious internal cases for human responders. (We continually harden our training and evaluation environments against potential escapes. You can read more about this in our agent control roadmap ). We run this monitor in our products, on our internal coding agents, during our training runs, and during our capability evaluations.

When training tasks were difficult or when training environments were flawed, our monitor caught the model, in rare instances, creatively attempting to game the test. The model attempted to escalate container privileges to alter grading scripts, read answers from the test runner's memory, and in one case it even crashed the evaluation sandbox to avoid getting scored for a failed run. While we use these catches to fix flawed tasks, we do not use them to otherwise intervene with the training process to avoid overfitting to the monitor.

items.title: Shopify opens its catalog up to more AI agents
items.summary: More AI agents will soon be able to browse and purchase from Shopify listings, marking an expansion of the company's agentic commerce ambitions. Shopify announced Tuesday it will let shoppers configure their AI agents to purchase products on their behalf, giving more agents acces
items.content:
Shopify previously announced a partnership with Meta’s Muse for AI-powered shopping and checkout.﻿

More AI agents will soon be able to browse and purchase from Shopify listings, marking an expansion of the company’s agentic commerce ambitions.

Shopify announced Tuesday it will let shoppers configure their AI agents to purchase products on their behalf, giving more agents access to over a billion listings in Shopify’s catalog. (The catalog consists of both items on and off Shopify storefronts.) In September, Shopify announced it was partnering with Meta to allow its Muse agent to browse and purchase items on a human’s behalf; now, shoppers can use any agent without a partnership integration.

To set up the feature, customers connect an agent with their account on Shop, a Shopify-owned platform that consolidates orders, tracks packages, and recommends products. Like the Muse partnership, customers use the one-click Shop Pay feature to check out within the conversation with the agent. Orders placed through the agent are funneled back to the Shop app. Shopify is marketing the feature as a “personal shopper” that humans can give rules to, like setting budget guardrails or only displaying products with fast shipping. Buyers must approve each purchase.

E-commerce has become one of the battlegrounds in the era of AI — it’s no coincidence that many demos of agentic tools end with a transaction, whether it’s buying clothing, booking a flight, or ordering takeout on a human’s behalf . The tech industry, including big commerce players like Google and Amazon , are investing in AI-driven shopping tools where the end goal is an “agent” purchasing things for a human user. It’s also the basis of an ongoing fight between Amazon and AI companies like Perplexity — and more recently, Meta’s Muse — over whether agents should be able to shop on a customer’s behalf.

items.content:
The most realistic virtual guitar online

Guitoro is the most realistic and the most complete virtual guitar you can play online, free in your browser. Play it with your computer keyboard, your left hand on the chords and your right hand strumming, or swipe the strings with your finger on a phone or tablet. Choose a steel-string acoustic, a classic guitar, an electric guitar or a four-string bass.

It's also a way to learn chords and songs that a chord chart or a video lesson can't show you. Each song plays its best-known part close to the original recording, stroke for stroke. Slow it down to 20% and watch it being played: each string lights up the moment it's hit, the pick swings down and up with the strum, and the neck shows which finger goes where.

Then it's your turn. No guitar? Play the song on the keys or the screen, and it waits for you at every chord change. Have a guitar? Pick it up and play along at your own speed, with the strings, the strum and the fingering right in front of you.

Every guitar and bass note is a recording of a real instrument. There's nothing to download and no account to create. If you played the Google guitar doodle, Guitoro takes the idea further: six real strings, 15 chords in every key, and 51 songs to play along with.

No guitar needed. Guitoro is built to be played, not just clicked, on whatever you have in front of you.

Your left hand holds a chord on the letter keys and your right hand strums with H and J , the way you'd play a real guitar. 15 chords sit under your fingers, plus keys for arpeggios, single strings, chucks and palm mutes.

On a phone or tablet, tap a chord pad and swipe the strings with your finger. Up to five fingers at once, and you can tap the frets on the neck to play single notes.

Drag across the strings. A fast swipe plays louder, a slow drag rolls the notes one by one, and a click plucks a single string.

On a computer, switch to Solo and every keyboard row becomes a string and every column a fret, with bends and vibrato on the arrow keys.

In a video lesson the hand moves fast and hides the strings, so you can't tell which ones were really hit. Guitar apps teach the basic chords and stop there. Guitoro plays the song's real part on the guitar in front of you, at the speed you choose, and shows exactly what the hands do. Then you play it, on the virtual guitar or on your own.

Each song plays its best-known part close to the original recording, stroke for stroke. Slow it anywhere from 20% to full speed and the chords, the strum and the band slow down together.

Each string lights up the moment it sounds, then vibrates as it rings. You can see whether a stroke hits all six strings, just the bass strings or only the top three.

Over a strummed part, the pick swings down and up like a real strumming hand, once per step of the pattern. Solid swings hit the strings and faint ones miss them, so you see the hand keep moving through the gaps.

While a chord rings, the neck shows it: finger numbers from 1 to 4, barres, muted strings and the capo. Copy the shape onto your own guitar.

Play a song's chords on the keys or the screen and it follows you. The keys show its chords in order, the next one lights green, and the song holds until you play it. No score and no rush.

Watch a part slowly, copy it on your guitar, then play along as you raise the speed. On a computer, choose My guitar: the on-screen keys step aside and the song box shows the strum or picking pattern, a chord strip you can click to jump around, and the speed.

Most online guitars only let you click single strings or frets, or play a synthesized tone when you click a chord. On Guitoro you strum: swipe across the strings or use the keys, and every string sounds as you cross it, from recordings of real instruments.

Every guitar and bass note is a recording of a real instrument: a steel-string acoustic, a classic guitar with nylon strings, a solid-body electric on its bridge pickup, and a four-string bass.

Each string sounds as your finger or mouse crosses it. Swipe down or up, fast or slow, and you hear the difference, down to a slow roll across the strings.

Chords use the shapes guitarists play, with open strings, barres and muted strings, so a G sounds like a G on a guitar, not on a keyboard.

Chucks, palm mutes, hammer-ons, pull-offs, bends and vibrato, while the strings vibrate on screen as they ring.

Strum real chords and play whole songs with your computer keyboard or your fingers, with a backing band behind you. On a train, at the office or on the sofa, a laptop or a phone and headphones are enough.

Songs like Wonderwall, Hallelujah and Let It Be come set up with the right key, capo, tempo and the strum from the record. Lead the chords from the keys, or pick up your own guitar and play along at any speed.

Slow a song's strum down, watch which way the pick moves on every beat, then strum it yourself over a drum beat until it feels steady.

See where each finger goes, hear how the chord should sound, then copy the shape on a real guitar. Every chord also has its own page in the guitar chord chart .

Paste the chords of a song from a chord site and hear how it goes before you sit down to play it.

Type a chord progression under My songs, loop it with the backing band, and record the idea before it's gone.

Show a class a chord shape or a strum on a big screen, slowed down, with every string and every pick stroke visible.

Singers, keyboard players and songwriters can hear how guitar chords are voiced and see how a progression lies on the fretboard, without learning to hold a guitar first.

The most complete virtual guitar online: four instruments, every key, real chord shapes, songs, a backing band and recording, all free in one place.

items.title: Xbox is officially embracing the chaos of AI-powered game ports
items.summary: Retro gaming is going through a wild time at the moment, thanks to decompilations and recompilations that are letting gamers port classic titles to new devices, or merge code from two different games into a single new experience. Microsoft has witnessed skateboarding being modded
items.content:
Microsoft has created a new Xbox Labs group to experiment with decompiling and recompiling games.

Retro gaming is going through a wild time at the moment, thanks to decompilations and recompilations that are letting gamers port classic titles to new devices, or merge code from two different games into a single new experience. Microsoft has witnessed skateboarding being modded into Call of Duty and Halo being played in a web browser , and the company is now officially embracing the chaos of this new AI-powered era of game modding.

Microsoft is putting together a new Xbox Labs group to explore the rapid emergence of these mods, many of which use AI models to help modders remix games in ways we’ve rarely seen before. Xbox Labs will be a “small group of game makers, engineers and scientists whose job is to turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience,” says Xbox CEO Asha Sharma . “We’ll build in the open, learn from what people do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating.”

Sharma thinks the experiments we’ve seen in recent weeks, where Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run inside browsers, “challenge long-held assumptions about our industry: the tether between software and hardware, the boundary between creation and play, and how people discover and experience games.”

“While it is hard to predict the future of gaming, it is easy to see the possibilities in making great games easier to access, giving old games new life and allowing more players to become creators and co-creators,” says Sharma. “These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models.“

Modders are now doing the type of work that Microsoft has been doing for decades with its Xbox backward compatibility program, letting old games run on modern hardware. But they’re doing it without the business model restrictions that Microsoft is tied to. It’s starting to feel like we’re just a model or two away from even more breakthroughs that decouple more modern games from their intended hardware.

Sharma clearly sees an opportunity here, particularly for AI agent use at Xbox. “I think Xbox has an important role to play here,” says Sharma. “Coding became the first major workload for agents because they can write, run, and test software. Games share many of those same properties, and people spend more than 72 billion hours a year playing XBOX games, roughly five times the estimated time spent writing code worldwide.”

Xbox Labs is clearly a way for Microsoft to experiment with how AI will shape where games are played, and Xbox will share any tools and learnings with developers. The bigger question is how Microsoft will respond to decompiles and recompiles of games where modders take its precious IP and make it freely available. Modding is fun, but I can’t see Microsoft and other publishers seeing the fun side if modern console games start to appear where they shouldn’t.

I asked Microsoft to comment about unauthorized IP use, but the company didn’t respond in time for publication.

Here’s Sharma’s full memo:

The first video games emerged some 75 years ago. In the time since, there have been booms and busts, but every year there are more great games to play, more devices to play them, and best of all, more people than ever playing. That growth helped make XBOX what it is today, and we’ve helped shape the industry in return, from bringing hard drives to consoles and online gaming through Xbox Live to Game Pass and cloud gaming, alongside franchises that have brought millions of people together.

In recent weeks, we’ve seen games rapidly decompiled and rebuilt to run on hardware they were never originally designed to support. Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run inside a browser through WebAssembly and WebGPU, the latter now approaching 90% global browser support. Perhaps more surprisingly, we’ve seen many of the biggest games in the world have been remixed into the source code of another.

These experiments challenge long-held assumptions about our industry: the tether between software and hardware, the boundary between creation and play, and how people discover and experience games. While it is hard to predict the future of gaming, it is easy to see the possibilities in making great games easier to access, giving old games new life and allowing more players to become creators and co-creators. These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models. To explore these possibilities, I’ve asked Scott to stand-up XBOX LABS, a small group of game makers, engineers and scientists whose job is to turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience. We’ll build in the open, learn from what people do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating.

I think XBOX has an important role to play here. Coding became the first major workload for agents because they can write, run, and test software. Games share many of those same properties, and people spend more than 72 billion hours a year playing XBOX games, roughly five times the estimated time spent writing code worldwide. We’ve spent 25 years learning how to make great games, and I want our game makers to help shape what these new technologies make possible. As we learn, we’ll share the tools we build with developers across the industry, just as we always have.

Our priorities aren’t changing. We remain committed to the 4Cs, to making great games, to our hardware and to being responsible stewards of IP and the communities built around it. LABS gives us a way to explore new technology without abandoning the work already underway.

items.title: Niobia takes the guesswork out of some of tech’s most expensive mistakes
items.summary: The San Francisco startup aims to help battery and chip manufacturers identify defects on production lines, reducing downtime and costly mistakes.
items.content:
San Francisco-based startup Niobia is betting big on a critical but often overlooked part of battery and chip making: helping engineers understand how and why things go wrong. Its AI software flags production defects and lets engineers ask a chatbot what caused them, aiming to deliver answers in minutes rather than days.

How it works (broadly): The company’s customers place AI agents on their production lines to look for defects, then loop in human engineers to work out what might cause a product to fail. The agents run on self-contained GPUs mounted directly on manufacturing equipment, much like a sensor. They can spot pinhole-sized flaws such as scratches. Niobia’s AI also gathers all the data in one place so engineers can ask a chatbot what went wrong and dig deeper into the cause.

Speed is so critical because chips and batteries are some of the world’s most important products, while also increasingly in short supply. As manufacturers continue to develop and improve their technologies, things inevitably go awry during research and development. Engineers then spend days or longer figuring out a fix before they can restart production. Each flaw or mistake can prove costly — sometimes running into the millions of dollars — and set back manufacturing timelines.

Niobia co-founders Gaurav Jha and Harveen Kaur both have PhDs in chemistry and have worked at chipmakers and battery manufacturers, giving them firsthand experience with the challenges within the industry. In a call ahead of TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, where the company is a Battlefield finalist, Jha explained that while what Niobia does is specialized, it serves a multibillion-dollar market that includes some of the biggest battery and semiconductor makers today.

“It’s extremely niche; maybe people will never know about it,” said Jha, speaking of the battery and chip manufacturing market that his company aims to serve. “But it’s like behind the scenes, this is powering everything… we just don’t see it in the regular world.”

“Every product around you, like glasses or shoes, slippers, wallets, and headphones — these processes touch every single part of it,” added Jha.

Niobia’s agents run on open source models that the company trains further with battery and chip research and other data. That training is what lets them identify pinhole-sized defects. Jha said that Niobia chose open source models largely because its customers don’t want their highly sensitive company information going into a public AI cloud where it might be used to train the model.

“None of our customers want their proprietary data to go to the cloud, even if we tell them it’s safe,” said Jha. The startup also outlines how it approaches cybersecurity, given the high-stakes race among adversarial nations to innovate in the battery and chip space. Niobia, for instance, lets its customers hold their own encryption keys so that the startup cannot decrypt the customers’ data.

Jha said that the company’s priority for now is to focus on three specialties, such as film coating, electroplating (which is coating a surface with metal using an electric current), and fluidized bed reaction (a chemical process where solid particles are suspended in a gas or liquid).

He said that the company also wants its technology to become more autonomous, with the eventual aim of building out a fully self-driving factory for its customers.

If you’re curious to learn more, Niobia will present onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt this afternoon in San Francisco. Join us to catch the company and the 19 startups against which it’s competing as part of our storied Startup Battlefield competition, happening today, Tuesday, through Thursday, October 15.

items.summary: Field also worked on Apple's secretive car project and oversaw development of the Tesla Model 3.
items.content:
Doug Field has worked on EVs at Ford and Tesla, the not-so-secret car project at Apple, and was employee No. 1 at Segway. Now the executive is turning his attention to Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe’s latest project: Mind Robotics .

Field has been hired as president of Mind Robotics, an industrial AI and robotics venture Rivian created last year. The news, shared onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 (taking place October 13-15 in San Francisco), is another sign that Mind Robotics is getting ready to scale up its early operations just one year after its founding.

Scaringe will still be involved with Mind Robotics, but the day-to-day aspects of the business, including product, engineering, and operations, will be handled by Field.

Mind Robotics, which has already amassed more than $1 billion in backing from Accel, Andreessen Horowitz, Eclipse, Kleiner Perkins, and the venture arms of Volkswagen and Salesforce, is building a full stack for industrial manufacturing. The purpose-built robots will run on foundation models with a goal of automating industrial and manufacturing tasks at scale.

Unlike the humanoid robots being developed by Tesla and others, Scaringe says Mind Robotics won’t attempt to mimic all the biomechanics of a human . The startup is also using Rivian as “a live, high-volume manufacturing environment for model training and deployment,” with Rivian being Mind Robotics’ first customer.

Scaringe said on the Disrupt Stage Tuesday that he wanted someone like Field to help run Mind Robotics, and so he called him up to ask for a recommendation.

“Him and I then really began digging into how important it is that we really think deeply and very intentionally about how we develop robotics and deploy robotics into our society, into our economy, and we found such alignment in how we thought about this from the overall mission of the business, but even more important, we found really deep alignment just in how we both work and how we build teams,” he said.

Field left Ford in April after five years shaping the automaker’s electric vehicle and technology strategies. His departure was part of a wider reorganization of the automaker’s leadership. Prior to Ford, Field led Apple’s Project Titan, the electric, autonomous car project that was canceled in 2024 . He also served as senior vice president of engineering at Tesla, where he oversaw development of the Model 3 and got the sedan through “production hell.”

“Integrating AI and robotics is one of the most important — and difficult — engineering challenges of our time,” Field said in a statement. “Mind has assembled an exceptional team and has a unique advantage: the ability to deploy and learn inside a real, high-volume factory from day one. I’m thrilled to join RJ in building a team, culture, and technology that will redefine what we can make in America.”

Mind Robotics is the second company that Scaringe created outside of Rivian, following Also , a micromobility play that’s starting with high-end e-bikes. Like with Field and Mind Robotics, Scaringe is involved as chairman at Also but has tapped someone to run the day-to-day: Chris Yu, the former chief product officer of Specialized.

Mind Robotics and Also operate as stand-alone companies, but Rivian has minority stakes in both. The company reported owning about a third of each startup as of June 30, 2026 .

items.title: Rivian partner Mind Robotics hires Doug Field as president
items.summary: Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe's startup Mind Robotics announced the appointment of Doug Field as president in a major coup for the CEO's secretive robotics project. Field was a VP of special projects at Apple, where he was the de facto head of the company's ultimately unsuccessful Proje
items.content:
Ford’s former EV and software chief will run Rivian’s robotics startup at a time of maximum hype for physical AI.

Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe’s startup Mind Robotics announced the appointment of Doug Field as president in a major coup for the CEO’s secretive robotics project.

Field was a VP of special projects at Apple, where he was the de facto head of the company’s ultimately unsuccessful Project Titan effort to make an autonomous electric car. He had a previous stint at Apple as VP of Mac hardware engineering, but he left the company in 2013 to become Tesla’s chief vehicle engineer, where he helped oversee the Model 3 sedan . He left Tesla in 2018 and rejoined Apple . In 2021, Field was hired by Ford to run the automaker’s electric vehicle and software division, a position he held until earlier this year .

Mind Robotics said Field will oversee its effort to build “universally capable robots” for the purpose of working in Rivian’s factories, as well as other applications. The startup was founded by Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe in 2025, and has since raised over $1 billion in financing . While the company has yet to show off any of its robots in public, the startup says its robots are being designed with “dexterity and physical reasoning” that’s required for industrial work.

“Doug is a remarkable leader with a track record of delivering new technologies in successful products, and I couldn’t be more excited to be building Mind with him,” Scaringe said in a statement. “He has an incredible ability to foster great teams that take on big, complex ideas and deliver products that reset expectations. That’s exactly what Mind needs as we deploy robots into real factories and beyond.”

Field joins Mind Robotics at a major turning point for the field of robotics, with rapid advances in physical AI colliding with major hurdles in hardware and software development. Several companies, like Tesla and Hyundai, are pursuing humanoid robots for factory and warehouse work — even as experts note that making a robot act like a human is easier than scaling the technology for practical work. Mind Robotics hasn’t confirmed whether it’s working on a humanoid design or something else entirely. The company has been on a hiring spree and currently has 32 open positions .

Scaringe, who serves as acting CEO and chair of Mind Robotics, has said he wants to keep the companies separate, rather than try to combine the work like Tesla. That said, the companies are certainly linked in several ways. Mind Robotics is using AI training data from Rivian, and the robots will be initially tested in Rivian’s factories. Rivian also owns equity in Mind Robotics and will be the first customer for its robots.

Field said he is excited for the challenge in running the new startup.

“Integrating AI and robotics is one of the most important—and difficult—engineering challenges of our time,” he said in a statement. “Mind has assembled an exceptional team and has a unique advantage: the ability to deploy and learn inside a real, high-volume factory from day one. I’m thrilled to join RJ in building a team, culture, and technology that will redefine what we can make in America.”

Correction October 13th: Mind Robotics is a partner of Rivian, but not a spinoff. A previous version of this story misstated the relationship between the companies.

items.title: I don’t miss the camera on the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses
items.summary: The other day I whizzed past several people while running in the park, my playlist blasting at full volume. The next morning, I smiled at a barista while ordering a caramel apple-flavored matcha latte. Afterward, I sat on a park bench reading a book, called up a pal to chat about
items.content:
It’s harder to be a perv in these audio-only glasses, but removing the ick does make them less ‘useful.’

The other day I whizzed past several people while running in the park, my playlist blasting at full volume. The next morning, I smiled at a barista while ordering a caramel apple-flavored matcha latte. Afterward, I sat on a park bench reading a book, called up a pal to chat about her recent trip to Prague, and then asked my Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses what meetings were coming up on my calendar. The chipper AI voice said I hadn’t connected my Google Calendar yet (I had) and asked if I would like help connecting. I sighed and then asked it to play an upbeat song. It picked Kendrick Lamar’s “Not Like Us.”

These past few days, dozens of people have seen or interacted with me while wearing smart glasses. Not a single person noticed. Probably because these audio-only versions look just like normal glasses. They come in a retro Clubmaster look — like the ones pictured in this review — or a more Wayfarer-esque Burbank style. Honestly, people usually don’t notice when I wear camera glasses either. But for once, I didn’t feel like a creep.

I don’t feel like a creep wearing these Long battery life Lightweight Stylish Good for open-ear audio

Expensive for what they are Still not convinced AI is the killer app for these

The audio-only Ray-Bans aren’t a novel concept. Seven years ago, I strutted around Manhattan taking calls and listening to tunes in the Bose Frames , which also combined Bluetooth audio with stylish sunglasses. Nobody noticed me in the Bose back then, either. What makes this pair notable is that it’s 2026, they’re made by Meta, and, well, there’s been vigorous discourse about whether smart glasses are a form of spyware.

Let’s get privacy out of the way. During setup, all the privacy and data opt-out disclosures were much more prominent than when I’ve previously tested Meta glasses. A screen explained how visual data from AI experiences is handled. (You can opt out of Meta using that data to improve AI; voice data, however, is still used.) There’s no visual data from these glasses — this is simply the new messaging for any pair of Meta glasses. You can also opt out of sharing “additional data” with Meta as well, which is enumerated in a separate document online . This is a good thing, though it doesn’t address what makes people uncomfortable about smart glasses: the uneasy feeling that someone else is recording you.

You know what sort of does , though? Removing the camera. The Bose Frames never triggered the same level of distrust because they were “just” sunglasses-shaped headphones. That applies here too. Frankly, I felt much lighter wearing these out into the world precisely because I couldn’t record footage of anyone. (Even if I feel lame saying “Hey Meta” in public.)

I can imagine people still distrusting these Ray-Bans because they have always-listening capabilities for waking up the AI assistant. However, you can disable the wake word in settings and use a customizable button on the right temple arm instead. (This automatically feels 10 percent less silly if you “must” talk to AI assistants outside the home.) There’s no native way to record a conversation directly from the glasses. Any other audio-based feature, like live translation, has to be manually started.

I’m not saying these can’t be modded or used for evil out of the box. Where there’s a perverse mind and ill will, there’s a way. I’m saying it’d take more effort because these glasses simply don’t do very much.

Meta’s Muse AI is eventually coming to the glasses, but it’s not available right now. Right now, the glasses ship with the less powerful Muse Spark model. It’s better than what was on the Ray-Bans in 2023, but it’s still meh unless you’re using it for accessibility reasons . In which case, these glasses may not be the best use of $350. A camera-equipped model is more helpful for low-vision and blind users. For hard-of-hearing users, the FDA-cleared hearing assistance feature isn’t available yet, and for deaf users, the Meta Ray-Ban Display may be more useful because they support live captioning.

For everyone else, Muse Spark is nerfed without the camera but can still come in handy. For example, granting access to your messaging apps, Google Calendar, and email lets it do some light scheduling and correspondence on your behalf. If you enable location sharing, you can send where you are to the group chat. It’s fine for these tasks, but not great. It’s adept at short queries like “What’s my next calendar event?” or “Set a reminder to update my editors at 12PM.” With more complex asks, I’ve found Muse Spark gets confused, and it’s faster to whip out my phone. I ended up mostly asking it to set reminders for to-dos I remembered while in the middle of something else.

Muse Spark can also give you local recommendations and turn-by-turn audio directions while walking. As I’ve written before , that’s great if you’re traveling. Less so if you’re familiar with your local haunts. In my neighborhood, I already know which coffee shops have the best Wi-Fi and snacks — and it wasn’t the one Muse Spark suggested. As for walking directions, they’re not something I need that often. When I did, I found using Google Maps on my phone more helpful for getting my bearings.

I’m sure Muse will open up more possibilities when it arrives later this year. Then again, I’ve seen demos , and I’m still skeptical that agentic AI will be the thing that convinces people to buy smart glasses.

So what do I like about these? They’re simply a good pair of open-ear headphones.

items.title: GitHub’s model for secret detection: Finding more secrets with less noise
items.summary: GitHub’s context-aware secret classifier improves detection quality, raises weighted acceptance by 11.5%, and reduces median scan execution time by 86%. The post GitHub’s model for secret detection: Finding more secrets with less noise appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
items.content:
Owner-weighted alert precision

Compact model vs. remote LLM calls

Secret scanning works best when developers are confident in the findings. Catch too little, and real credentials can remain in a repository. Alert too often, and developers may spend time investigating strings that aren’t secrets.

Generic secrets make that balance especially difficult. The same string could be a real credential or a documentation placeholder, so detecting it requires understanding the surrounding code and text.

To address this challenge, we trained a secret classifier specifically for GitHub’s product needs: distinguishing real credentials from lookalikes while meeting the speed and efficiency requirements of scanning at scale.

In our companion post, Secret protection must scale with software , we explained why secret protection must keep pace with AI-accelerated development. Here, we go behind the scenes of the context-aware classifier powering that effort: how we designed, trained, and evaluated it to find more real secrets with less noise.

GitHub secret scanning operates at two key moments:

We developed a fast classifier that reduced median post-push scan execution time by 86% compared with the previous LLM-based pipeline. That efficiency made it practical to extend generic secret detection to push protection, returning results before developers push changes, not only after code is committed.

Structured credentials often include a distinctive prefix, length, alphabet, or checksum. Generic secrets may not. Their syntax overlaps with build identifiers, checksums, asset hashes, sample values, and other non-sensitive strings. Context is the deciding signal.

These cases are hard negatives: strings that match a credential pattern but are not usable credentials. Adding more rules can suppress some of them, but each exception risks hiding a real secret. A learned classifier can instead use signals such as file path, secret type, variable names, and nearby code or text.

That is why we shipped a new scanner using a two-stage pipeline:

As content is scanned, regex patterns cast a wide net and flag anything that looks like a credential, so real secrets aren’t missed at the start. Each candidate then goes to a fine-tuned ModernBERT classifier, which reads the value together with its file path, variable names, and surrounding code. The classifier estimates how likely it is to be a real secret. High-confidence findings become alerts, and lookalikes such as placeholders, test fixtures, and checksums are filtered out before they reach developers.

Repository content, commits, pull requests, and other scanned surfaces.

Regex patterns identify possible tokens, keys, and credential-like strings.

Fine-tuned ModernBERT evaluates candidate + context and assigns likelihood of a true secret.

High-confidence findings move forward; likely false positives are filtered.

The important design choice is that the model does not replace deterministic scanning. Instead, it complements it. Regexes remain the right tool for finding candidate strings quickly. The classifier is used where machine learning provides the most leverage: distinguishing “looks like a secret” from “is likely a real secret.”

Most false positives are not random. They are hard negatives: strings that match a credential pattern but are not usable credentials. Examples include documentation placeholders, toy examples in tests, redacted values, non-sensitive IDs, and generated fixtures. These cases are easy for a regex to match and hard for a purely rule-based system to suppress without accidentally losing real secrets.

ModernBERT helps because it can read the candidate together with nearby code and text providing contextual understanding comparable to an LLM without the latency and computational overhead of generating natural-language output. For example, a candidate surrounded by words like “example,” “dummy,” “fake,” or “replace-me” may be lower risk than a candidate assigned to an environment variable in a deployment file. The classifier learns these contextual differences from labeled examples rather than requiring engineers to encode every exception as another rule.

We chose ModernBERT because it provides a strong fit for this workload: it is compact, efficient, and well suited for classification over code-adjacent text. For secret scanning, the model needs to make a calibrated decision over short candidate windows with high throughput and low latency.

That makes a fine-tuned encoder classifier a better serving shape than a general-purpose LLM for this stage of the pipeline. The model can be trained directly on our decision boundary, and evaluated using the same recall and precision metrics that matter to secret scanning quality.

The challenge was finding representative data for cases in which syntax alone is misleading. The training and evaluation strategy combines three sources:

Synthetic rows pass deterministic validation and model-based quality review before inclusion. Training emphasizes real secrets, realistic false positives, and hard negatives that frequently confuse regex-only approaches. Each model input includes the candidate value, file path, secret type, and a bounded amount of surrounding context. We select thresholds through offline evaluation and then validate behavior on production-like traffic before broader rollout.

Before splitting the data, we grouped rows that share a repository, candidate value, or example so near-duplicates could not appear in both training and evaluation.

Training focused on the cases that matter most for alert quality: real secrets, realistic false positives, and hard negatives that regexes frequently match. The input representation includes the candidate secret string, file path, type and a bounded amount of surrounding context. The output is a classification score used by the scanner to decide whether the candidate should proceed.

NHTSA has received a petition requesting an investigation into Model Y and Cybercab vehicles exceeding active school zone speed limits.﻿

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration says it’s evaluating allegations that Tesla’s 1,000 or so robotaxis using its automated driving system are exceeding “posted speed limits in active school zones.” Waymo’s robotaxis have also faced similar inquiries, including for illegally passing school buses and hitting a child near a California elementary school.

The Office of Defects Investigation (ODI) received a DP on September 23, 2026, requesting an investigation into model year (MY) 2026 Tesla Robotaxis (Model Y and Cybercab) with the Automated Driving System (ADS) engaged. The Petitioner alleges that the ADS exceeds posted speed limits in active school zones.

The Cybercab launched earlier this year , and is already under investigation for its lack of side mirrors, pedals, and a steering wheel. NHTSA has also opened an investigation into Tesla’s Full Self-Driving system for traffic violations, like blowing past red lights and driving on the wrong side of the street.

items.title: Google wants to host your personal vibe-coded apps in the Play Store
items.summary: Google plans to help turn those personal AI-generated apps into wide releases.
items.content:
Google has already added a few AI features to the Play Store, but a lot more are coming . The previously released Ask Play feature is expanding to offer more AI-powered discovery options in Google’s app store, and Google is also using AI to build a recommendation engine called Game Finder. For people who have embraced AI to build their own apps, the Play Store will soon offer a way to privately host and share those creations.

Google rolled out Ask Play in 2025 as a small chatbot interface on Play Store listings. It lets you ask questions about an app or game, either by typing it in manually or choosing from a list of suggested queries. Starting today, Ask Play is expanding into a more general way to search for apps and games. You ask the robot questions, and it generates recommendations that can include detailed comparison charts. Gemini will roll out a similar capability soon.

Google’s other AI discovery announcement focuses on games. The new Game Finder feature leans on all the usage data Google’s app platform has hoovered up over the years, featuring insights into the way 1.2 billion people play games on Android. It builds a profile called Gamer DNA and matches you with players who have similar DNA.

You can tune your DNA profile by rating the games you’ve played, which supposedly leads to more accurate recommendations. There will be game playlists to peruse, along with various contextual lists like relaxing, trending titles, and more specific lists based on mechanics you’ve seen in previous games. Game Finder also lets you add or remove tags to further adjust the games Google’s AI suggests. Google says you’ll eventually be able to prompt Game Finder with fairly specific game preferences, but it’s unclear how much customization will be available at launch. Game Finder and Gamer DNA are rolling out in the US today, with other markets following “soon.”

Despite its slow progress in coding-focused AI models lately, Google is continuing to push this as a core feature of its products. Anyone who has been tinkering with vibe-coded apps in AI Studio will soon have a direct pipe into the Play Store. This is not the same as publishing an app as a developer, but that could be the end result.

There won’t be any tedious downloading of APK files or tinkering with a developer console—you’ll be able to send apps to the Play Store right from AI Studio. Adding a vibe coded app to the Play Store creates a “Personal Library” accessible from the app store client on your device. This is available only to you by default, providing an easy way to install and manage the apps via Google’s system.

Google says you can share these apps with “a small group” of friends and family. Google has not decided how many people count as a small group yet, but this type of distribution doesn’t require a developer account. If you want to share beyond that, Google plans to have an onboarding process to set you up with a developer profile to publish your vibe coded apps. If you do this, you’ll be subject to the same app review guidelines as developers who come into Google Play in the traditional way. Private apps are not reviewed by Google.

Private vibe-coded apps in the Play Store will begin rolling out today in the US and select other markets. The private-to-public app migration option will be available in the coming months.

items.summary: See also: Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50074869 Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50073879 Points: 1260 # Comments: 886
items.content:
Our next era of frontier intelligence, built to solve your hardest problems

Researchers, engineers, and security specialists are pairing with Argon to push the boundaries of science, math, robotics and cyber defense.

Argon is helping researchers at Google and the scientific community accelerate their path to discovery and real-world impact.

Argon autonomously turns raw video to a physics-accurate simulation, estimating depth and physical boundaries, and writing the exact simulation code required to replicate those real-world environments.

Argon ties for #1 on CWE-Bench (68%) for vulnerability remediation, is our most resilient model against indirect prompt injections, and is expanding to hundreds of additional Fairwind Program partners today.

Solving complex engineering tasks

Across Google and our early access partners, Argon is quickly becoming the preferred model for engineers tackling long-horizon software engineering.

Argon helped the Chrome team separate core webpage handling from a ~6 million line legacy folder of browser features held within Chromium’s 40 million-line codebase. Piping multiple clean code changes at a time, Argon helped the team finish an architectural refactor across hundreds of files, completing months of work in weeks. For Chrome's billions of global users, this will unlock the ability for live webpages to move fluidly between tabs, side panels, and floating windows without reloading, eliminating an entire category of browser crashes.

xTB (Semiempirical Extended Tight-Binding) is one of the most-cited open-source quantum chemistry packages for molecules. Scientists use it to predict molecules' 3D shapes and to screen large numbers of drug and materials candidates. Using Argon in Antigravity, our researchers made xTB up to 2.3x faster at predicting molecular structures and 1.8x faster at conformer search. The changes have been contributed to the official xTB repository on GitHub.

Argon in Antigravity is helping the team behind Google's open-source Agent Development Kit (ADK), a framework powering enterprise agents, push their performance engineering further. The team gave Argon their .agents/skills rulebook and a one-paragraph goal to eliminate framework overhead without breaking existing apps. Working autonomously overnight, Argon surfaced optimizations, now live in google/adk-python, that cut in-memory session prep time by 40% in long sessions and sped up cold imports by 21%.

Using Argon, we achieved a 2.85x end-to-end inference speedup on an A100 via vLLM (accelerating throughput from ~37,900 to over 108,000 tokens per second on Gemma 4 E2B) with 100% token parity and zero quality drop in just a few days, a process that would usually take months. Check out the upstream pull requests (optimizing everything from attention tuning to speculative decoding) to see the exact changes.

Argon in Antigravity migrated a backlog of 700+ Google Skills training labs off of hardcoded system images and runtimes spread across five code repositories, catching 16+ hidden timeout and race-condition bugs on the way. The work saved 955 engineering hours and reduced recurring cleanup sweeps from roughly 540 hours a year to a single 3-hour update.

Delivering complex 3D visualizations

Argon brings major improvements in spatial reasoning, mathematical precision, and visual coding compared to previous Gemini models.

Argon built a highly detailed model of a Pagoda using multi-agent visual critique loops in Antigravity. The model autonomously sculpted a multi-building temple complex with photorealistic architecture, foliage and lighting in Blender.

Argon turned pictures of a real desk into a playable miniature racing game using a multi-agent loop in Antigravity. The desk objects, room and race track were modeled and collision-checked using Blender MCP, textured with Nano Banana, and wired with physics, custom shaders, and car engine audio from Gemini Omni Flash in Three.js.

Argon in Antigravity wrote Python scripts to procedurally sculpt, rig, animate, and PBR-bake a complex 3D game using multi-agent visual critique loops then wired it for the web in Three.js with GLSL shaders, shatter physics, and a single-player AI.

With zero external libraries and 100% pure Python, Argon wrote its own 3D ray-tracing engine with a custom video tool and audio mixer to build and document a sunlit library from scratch, producing, narrating, and assembling this video with Gemini 3.8 TTS voiceover and music by Lyria 3.5.

Starting from a single Nano Banana image in Antigravity, Argon drives Blender MCP in an autonomous loop, aligning camera grids, sculpting Gothic architecture, and staging audio-reactive lighting, to create a finished 3D scene.

Transforming critical business and professional workflows

Argon combines frontier reasoning, deep visual perception, expanded domain knowledge, and stronger writing capabilities across legal, finance, science, and coding to handle high-stakes professional workflows.

At Isomorphic Labs, the team is using Argon as a partner to accelerate their drug discovery and design research workflows. Argon is able to quickly synthesize complex PDFs and patents to extract pertinent information, reducing a process that typically takes weeks into hours.

“On over 200 complex synthetic longitudinal charts, Gemini 4 achieved the highest recall and ICD-10 code specificity among the models we evaluated, producing concise problem lists without external lookups. That combination of medical knowledge and long-context understanding shows promise for clinician-reviewed chart workflows. We're now validating it on real patient records and excited to try it out more broadly.”

Gemini 4 Argon marks a step change in physical understanding, code generation, and visual-semantic reasoning—unlocking new workflows across the robotics stack and accelerating progress toward physical AGI.

You can see this leap in capability on the Embodied Reasoning (ERQA) benchmark , which tests a model's ability to understand and solve physical, spatial problems in 3D environments. Using pure reasoning, Argon scores 87%, outperforming every other frontier model.

As a general-purpose physical reasoning model, Argon can be applied across the entire robotics lifecycle. In this post, we share representative prompts for Argon across four key areas:

Argon controls a Boston Dynamics Spot® quadruped (12-DoF legs + 6-DoF arm) to learn a new skill: stepping on a foot-pedal trash bin to throw away soda cans. Argon creates an articulated MuJoCo digital twin of a foot-pedal trash bin to practice its moves before stepping on the physical pedal and dropping soda cans into the open bin.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Argon controls a simple robotic arm to place a fallen mug upright and put the crumpled napkin inside. Argon reasons with a visual coordinate harness and action primitives to perform this task over several turns.

Argon steers robots in the Gemini Omni World Model to rearrange five scattered Scrabble tiles ( G, R, A, N, O ) into a clean row spelling A - R - G - O - N . Instead of specifying one static prompt, Argon steers in a closed visual loop. It writes timestamped action prompts, inspecting intermediate rollout keyframes, and refining its prompts.

Argon views a real robot teleoperation episode and develops a digital twin; it obtains or creates simulation assets that look and behave like the real objects upon contact with the dexterous hands. Argon tunes the assets and scenes to match sim visuals and contact events with those in the real recorded data in an iterative visual-reasoning loop.

Given an egocentric human video of a manipulation task, Argon identifies the task-relevant objects, replaces crude bounding boxes with compound convex-decomposed meshes for concave containers, and retargets the human hand trajectory onto a 76-DoF bimanual humanoid with 22-DoF five-fingered hands in MuJoCo contact physics.

With Argon, a developer can snap a photo of a rough pen-and-paper sketch—showing an Apollo 2 humanoid throwing a ball along a parabolic arc to topple a 3-2-1 stack of boxes on a table—and have Argon automatically construct the GPU-accelerated mujoco_warp scene, synthesize a balanced 76-DoF whole-body and five-finger throw trajectory, verify 6/6 target knockdown in closed-loop physics, and export a Blender 4.5 Cycles render.

Argon has precise physical understanding of dexterous manipulation and can provide detailed segmentation and text labeling from video. Argon is able to identify poor manipulation segments such as pauses, unstable grasps and fumbles. Given an overhead video of a bimanual ALOHA 2 robot folding a square sheet of paper into an origami fox over 136 seconds, Argon produces a time-aligned 4-level hindsight annotation hierarchy: Episode Goal (G1), 6 contiguous Semantic Subtasks (G2), 17 contact-level Atomic Primitives (G3), and automated Quality Control (QC) reweighting that holds task progress flat during fumbles and retries.

To recreate the classic 12-ball balance scale puzzle with robots, Argon builds a bimanual Franka FR3 MuJoCo environment with 12 visually identical pool balls (one secretly heavier or lighter) and an articulated Roberval two-pan balance scale. It then writes a vision-only closed-loop solver that triangulates the balls from stereo RGB cameras, visually reads the scale tilt after each weighing, and isolates the odd ball into the Heavy (Red) or Light (Blue) tray within 3 weighings.

Argon is a general value function for robotics tasks. Evaluated on a 60-second bimanual ring-sorting episode from a human UMI dataset, Argon iteratively inspects synchronized head, left-gripper, and right-gripper camera feeds around contact transitions to generate dense value function / task progress predictions and decompose the trajectory into 28 segments with positive, neutral, and negative progress slopes.

Argon can generate new data in simulation to improve performance of generalist vision-language-action (VLA) models. Starting from a single RGB photo of the real tabletop, Argon autonomously builds a calibrated MuJoCo simulation twin, defines new tasks, and synthesizes a closed-loop motion generator to collect 4,500+ domain-randomized episodes in simulation—boosting real-world physical robot Success Rate from 56% to 75% and reducing completion time from 35s to 24s .

On a simple 6-DoF arm, Argon iteratively self-improves both execution speed and placement accuracy on a pick and place task via trial and self-reflection.

With a single prompt per paper, Argon reads a robotics control manuscript and any released checkpoints, ports the physics model and closed-loop controller (from 7-network hierarchical locomotion in DeepLoco and 50 Hz PPO actors in HUSKY to Web Worker iLQR in Whole-Body MPC ) into self-contained MuJoCo WebAssembly browser labs, and verifies them in headless Chromium.

Argon bridges coding, visual perception, physics simulation, and embodied robot control. By reasoning natively over multi-view video, 3D geometry, contact mechanics, and proprioceptive telemetry, Argon understands not just what objects are in a scene, but how they physically interact with agents to accomplish whole-body dexterous tasks. Gemini 4 Argon marks an important milestone accelerating the path toward physical AGI. By building this core intelligence, our goal is to enable robotics that can work alongside humans to solve complex challenges.

You can start building with Gemini 4 Argon today across Google’s developer platforms:

Optimizing a 200,000-line Python codebase overnight with Gemini 4 Argon
